variants.title: Give every signal one job
variants.context: Curation gives every signal one job. Verify content identity from the bytes, measure candidate signals with their model and preprocessing versions, apply governed policies as explicit rules, then evaluate slices and approve one immutable manifest.
variants.prompt: A crawled image-text pair enters the curation pipeline. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Store alignment, predicted aesthetics, language, policy, watermark, and OCR outputs with their model and preprocessing versions.
Decode in a bounded environment and record cryptographic and perceptual hashes, dimensions, media type, and fetch evidence.
Evaluate explicit safety, rights, provenance, duplication, resolution, and representation rules as separate decisions.
Compare before and after slices, approve one immutable manifest, materialize shards, and preserve removal lineage.

variants.hint: Which fact does every later record have to point at?
variants.explanation: Identity comes first because scores and policy decisions bind to a content hash, not to a mutable URL.

variants.title: Give every signal one job
variants.context: Curation gives every signal one job. Verify content identity from the bytes, measure candidate signals with their model and preprocessing versions, apply governed policies as explicit rules, then evaluate slices and approve one immutable manifest.
variants.prompt: A refetch of an indexed URL returns different bytes than the last edition. Put the stages in order for the new fetch.

items.text: Run the safety, rights, and duplication rules against the new record rather than inheriting the old decision.
Fetch into quarantine, hash the new bytes, and observe that the hash does not match the prior manifest row.
Score the new content on its own, recording the scorer versions that produced each value.
Publish a successor manifest that carries the new edition and leaves the earlier release reproducible.

variants.hint: Mutable bytes create a new identity, not an update to an old one.
variants.explanation: Different bytes are a different sample, so every signal and decision is recomputed and the prior manifest stays intact.

variants.title: Give every signal one job
variants.context: Curation gives every signal one job. Verify content identity from the bytes, measure candidate signals with their model and preprocessing versions, apply governed policies as explicit rules, then evaluate slices and approve one immutable manifest.
variants.prompt: The aesthetic predictor is upgraded to a new version. Put the stages in order for the affected pool.

items.text: Re-evaluate the inclusion policies using the new scores as separate inputs.
Write a new score version beside the old one instead of overwriting the previous score column.
Compare inclusion changes by slice and approve a successor manifest if the evidence supports it.
Confirm the content hashes are unchanged, so identity does not need to be re-established.

variants.hint: A scorer upgrade changes measurement, not the bytes it measured.
variants.explanation: Scorer upgrades create new evidence rather than rewriting history, so old manifests stay reproducible.

variants.title: Test a filter like a model change
variants.context: A filter is a model intervention, so a proposed policy is tested like one: freeze the pool and scorer versions, compare distributions before and after each stage, inspect errors near the threshold, measure slices, train a bounded pilot, and record who approved the trade-off and what would reverse it.
variants.prompt: A team proposes a new inclusion policy for the next release. Put the evaluation steps in order.

items.text: Train a bounded pilot and evaluate downstream quality, safety, robustness, and memorization.
Measure modality, language, source, geography, and task-relevant slices.
Review the false positives and false negatives that sit near the threshold.
Freeze the candidate pool and the scorer versions so the comparison has a fixed baseline.
Record who approved the trade-off and what evidence would trigger reversal.
Compare counts and score distributions before and after every stage of the policy.

variants.hint: Nothing can be compared until something is held fixed.
variants.explanation: Filtering changes the training distribution, so it is evaluated as an intervention with a frozen baseline and a downstream pilot.

variants.title: Test a filter like a model change
variants.context: A filter is a model intervention, so a proposed policy is tested like one: freeze the pool and scorer versions, compare distributions before and after each stage, inspect errors near the threshold, measure slices, train a bounded pilot, and record who approved the trade-off and what would reverse it.
variants.prompt: Someone wants to raise the aesthetic floor by half a point. Put the steps that justify or block the change in order.

items.text: Write down who accepted the remaining trade-off and which drift would reverse it.
Read a sample of pairs just above and just below the new floor to see what the cut actually removes.
Chart how many pairs the higher floor removes and how the score distribution shifts.
Pin the same candidate pool and the same predictor version used by the current release.
Break the retained set down by language, source, and visual style to expose slices that collapse.
Train a bounded pilot on the stricter pool and compare downstream behavior with the prior manifest.

variants.hint: A count is not evidence until you know which shapes it removed.
variants.explanation: The threshold review comes before the slice review, because you cannot judge a cut you have not looked at.

variants.title: Test a filter like a model change
variants.context: A filter is a model intervention, so a proposed policy is tested like one: freeze the pool and scorer versions, compare distributions before and after each stage, inspect errors near the threshold, measure slices, train a bounded pilot, and record who approved the trade-off and what would reverse it.
variants.prompt: A language filter is proposed to drop captions the detector cannot classify. Put the evaluation steps in order.

items.text: Report retention per language slice rather than one aggregate number.
Pilot-train and check downstream behavior on the languages the filter touched.
Record the approver and the retention drift that would force a rerun.
Freeze the pool, the language detector version, and its preprocessing.
Inspect low-confidence detections to see which real languages the detector abstains on.
Compare retained counts before and after the filter at each stage.

variants.hint: The step that exposes representation damage is not the step that counts pairs.
variants.explanation: Aggregate counts can stay healthy while a language slice disappears, so the slice measurement is a separate required step.

variants.title: Measure what the filter removed
variants.context: Aggregate retention can look healthy while one slice collapses. Slice retention is that slice's surviving pairs divided by its candidates, and the slice-retention gap is its distance from the aggregate rate. Successive floors each apply to what the previous stage left.
variants.prompt: A candidate pool of 5,000,000 pairs retains 3,000,000 after filtering. One language slice holds 40,000 candidates and 10,000 of them survive. What is that slice's retention, in percent?
variants.hint: A slice is measured against its own candidates, not against the pool.
variants.explanation: Slice retention is the slice's survivors over its own candidates, so 10,000 of 40,000 is 25 percent.

mistakes.feedback: That is the aggregate retention rate, which is exactly the number the slice measurement exists to challenge.
That is the share removed from the slice, not the share retained.

variants.title: Measure what the filter removed
variants.context: Aggregate retention can look healthy while one slice collapses. Slice retention is that slice's surviving pairs divided by its candidates, and the slice-retention gap is its distance from the aggregate rate. Successive floors each apply to what the previous stage left.
variants.prompt: A release retains 62 percent of the pool overall. An illustration slice holds 60,000 candidates and retains 18,000. How large is the slice-retention gap, in percentage points?
variants.hint: Compute the slice rate first, then compare it with the aggregate rate.
variants.explanation: The slice retains 30 percent against an aggregate 62 percent, so the gap is 32 percentage points.

mistakes.feedback: That is the slice retention itself, not its distance from the aggregate rate.
That subtracts the slice retention from 100, which measures removal rather than the gap.

variants.title: Measure what the filter removed
variants.context: Aggregate retention can look healthy while one slice collapses. Slice retention is that slice's surviving pairs divided by its candidates, and the slice-retention gap is its distance from the aggregate rate. Successive floors each apply to what the previous stage left.
variants.prompt: A shard holds 250,000 pairs. Raising the aesthetic floor removes 18 percent of them, then a resolution floor removes 10 percent of what is left. How many pairs survive?
variants.hint: The second floor only sees what the first floor passed.
variants.explanation: Stages compose in order, so 250,000 times 0.82 is 205,000, and 205,000 times 0.90 is 184,500.

mistakes.feedback: That stops after the aesthetic floor and never applies the resolution floor.
That subtracts 28 percent of the original pool, treating both floors as if they saw the same base.

variants.title: Refuse the collapsed decision
variants.context: A high aesthetic score can still describe an unsafe, duplicated, miscaptioned, unlicensed, or unrepresentative pair. Quality, safety, provenance, and representation decisions stay independent, and none of them is granted by accessibility or by a similarity score.
variants.prompt: A pair scores well on aesthetics and alignment, but its content hash matches a restricted-identity list. A teammate argues the strong scores should win. What is correct?
options: Include it, since two independent scorers agree the pair is high quality.
Include it but flag the row so a reviewer can revisit the restriction later.
Exclude it, because a restricted-identity match is a policy decision scores cannot override.
optionFeedback: Quality scorers were never trained to answer the safety question the hash list answers.
Shipping the pair while the review is pending puts restricted content into the shards anyway.
Correct: safety keeps a durable restricted-identity path so removed content cannot re-enter from another crawl.
variants.hint: Which of these signals was built to answer the question actually being asked?
variants.explanation: Quality, safety, provenance, and representation stay independent, so a high score never overrides a policy decision.

variants.title: Refuse the collapsed decision
variants.context: A high aesthetic score can still describe an unsafe, duplicated, miscaptioned, unlicensed, or unrepresentative pair. Quality, safety, provenance, and representation decisions stay independent, and none of them is granted by accessibility or by a similarity score.
variants.prompt: A proposal blends aesthetics, alignment, and policy outputs into one composite quality score, and inclusion is gated on that single number. What is the main problem?
options: The composite needs recalibration whenever the candidate pool grows.
The composite is expensive to recompute whenever any one scorer is upgraded.
The composite lets a strong quality signal mask a failing safety or rights decision.
optionFeedback: Pool growth affects calibration for every scheme, including one that keeps the fields separate.
Recompute cost is real but it is not what makes the release unsafe.
Correct: independent decisions must not be collapsed, because averaging hides the one that should block inclusion.
variants.hint: What can a high average conceal about the individual inputs?
variants.explanation: Never collapse independent quality, safety, provenance, and representation decisions into one score.

variants.title: Refuse the collapsed decision
variants.context: A high aesthetic score can still describe an unsafe, duplicated, miscaptioned, unlicensed, or unrepresentative pair. Quality, safety, provenance, and representation decisions stay independent, and none of them is granted by accessibility or by a similarity score.
variants.prompt: A team wants to mark pairs as cleared for training whenever the crawler fetched them without authentication and the source page carried no notice. What is correct?
options: Accept the rule but require an aesthetics floor so only useful pairs are cleared this way.
Treat rights as a separate reviewed decision with legal and policy owners.
Accept the rule, since public accessibility is what makes a crawl lawful in the first place.
optionFeedback: An aesthetics floor answers a preference question and has nothing to say about rights.
Correct: permission, consent, and ownership are not inferable from accessibility or from recorded provenance.
Reachability describes a server configuration, not a grant of permission to train.
variants.hint: Does being able to fetch something tell you anything about permission to use it?
variants.explanation: Rights and consent are jurisdiction-specific reviewed decisions, never a byproduct of accessibility or a similarity score.

variants.title: Give each signal its question
variants.context: Each measurement answers one narrow question. Alignment asks whether an embedding model sees related semantics, predicted aesthetics asks what a learned preference model expects from its rating data, policy classifiers judge the defined harm policy, and the content hash is what every fact binds to.
variants.prompt: Match each signal to the one question it answers.

pairs.label: Image-text alignment
pairs.detail: Does an embedding model see related semantics between this caption and this image?

pairs.label: Predicted aesthetics
pairs.detail: Would a preference model trained on rating data expect high ratings for this image?

pairs.label: Policy classifier
pairs.detail: Does this content fall inside the defined harm policy for this release?

pairs.label: Content hash
pairs.detail: Which exact bytes should every score and decision on this row bind to?

variants.hint: Only one of these is an identity, not a measurement.
variants.explanation: Each signal answers one narrow question, so overlapping them is what lets a strong score stand in for a decision it cannot make.

variants.title: Give each signal its question
variants.context: Each measurement answers one narrow question. Alignment asks whether an embedding model sees related semantics, predicted aesthetics asks what a learned preference model expects from its rating data, policy classifiers judge the defined harm policy, and the content hash is what every fact binds to.
variants.prompt: Match each signal to what it explicitly does not establish.

pairs.label: Image-text alignment
pairs.detail: It does not prove the caption is factually true about the image.

pairs.label: Predicted aesthetics
pairs.detail: It does not measure universal beauty, only the preferences in its rating data.

pairs.label: Policy classifier
pairs.detail: It does not grant rights, consent, or permission to train on the pair.

pairs.label: Content hash
pairs.detail: It does not say anything about who authored or owns the bytes it identifies.

variants.hint: Ask what a stakeholder might wrongly read into each signal.
variants.explanation: Each signal has a boundary, and most curation failures come from reading one signal as an answer to a neighboring question.

variants.context: Each measurement answers one narrow question. Alignment asks whether an embedding model sees related semantics, predicted aesthetics asks what a learned preference model expects from its rating data, policy classifiers judge the defined harm policy, and the content hash is what every fact binds to.
variants.prompt: Match each signal to the failure that appears when it is missing or unversioned.

pairs.label: Image-text alignment
pairs.detail: Captioned pairs enter training with text unrelated to the picture.

pairs.label: Predicted aesthetics
pairs.detail: Inclusion changes after an upgrade cannot be attributed, because scores were overwritten in place.

pairs.label: Policy classifier
pairs.detail: Restricted content re-enters from a later crawl because nothing judged the harm policy.

pairs.label: Content hash
pairs.detail: A mutated URL silently reassigns old scores to new bytes.

variants.hint: Trace the failure back to the one field that would have caught it.
variants.explanation: Every recorded signal exists to catch a specific failure, which is why they are versioned and stored separately.
